articles.title: Progressives Must Rethink Race
articles.author: Tom Hall
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. It’s time for Americans, including progressives, to try new thinking about race. The right-wing e-newsletter The Dispatch called the midterms “A Blowout.” The Donald’s immediate response was to double down on the politics of division and to appoint extreme racist Stephen Miller as his chief of staff for the remainder of his term. Much of the “progressive” response to the midterms has been a mixture of gloating, recriminations about the “Democratic Party Machine,” and announced plans for retribution—against both enemies and natural allies. At the October 2–4 Left Coast Forum in Los Angeles, a conservatively dressed, gray-haired gentleman with a complexion darker than Herschel Walker’s sat in the back row of several sessions. He didn’t speak most of the time, but when he did, he was soft-spoken and not confrontational. When I approached him, he identified himself as an MSW and a social policy analyst. One issue came to the fore each time I spoke to him or heard him speak during a session. He asserted that “race” is a false construct and that focusing on it risks distracting us from the real problems and issues facing society. Science has pretty well eliminated any objective basis for racial classifications. Even before European mercantilism and colonialism initiated global mass trading that mixed heretofore separate population groups and civilizations, people were people. We share essentially 100% identical DNA, regardless of individual variations in gene expression affecting eye color, skin pigmentation, perceived “beauty,” handedness, disease susceptibility, and a million other characteristics. Related: What If AI Learns That Inequality—not Humanity—is the Problem? People descended from other primates that lived in groups. And people, from their earliest manifestations, have been group-focused primates. As small groups merged into villages, then cities and states, they retained their group identities and practiced behaviors that pitted groups against other groups, both for survival and for gain. This pattern is not unique to evil Caucasian colonists trying to subjugate Africans, Asians, Latin Americans, and Native Americans. It is what history and science tell us about humans on every continent, humans of every color, and humans of every political persuasion, going back as far as archaeological remains reveal evidence of group living, group warfare, and individual violence. “Race” as a social definition is much more recent and is essentially an economic rather than a scientific or social reality. As early as 1640, a Virginia colonial court sentenced a Black man to lifetime servitude while sentencing his White co-defendants to only extended indenture. And in 1661, Virginia started crafting laws to officially recognize “race-based” slavery. These were decisions of economic policy, not scientific reality. American slavery was novel. Spain instituted slavery across the Caribbean, first trying to coerce Native Americans into providing labor as part of purported religious instruction and conversion. But Native Americans had the home-court advantage and easily disappeared into forests and jungles when they didn’t want to be slaves. Following Christopher Columbus’s example of seizing people from lands he explored, traders traveling to Africa seized Africans and brought them to the New World. The Africans didn’t have the Native Americans’ local knowledge or connections to local tribes that might have enabled them to escape bondage. And the traders had many customers eager for captive workers who had no opportunities for escape. So the 1661 Virginia slavery legislation was a formalization of an emerging economic system that used an artificial and unscientific basis for providing legal economic benefits to plantation owners. Then, a 1662 Virginia law held that “Black” children’s status followed that of their mother rather than their father. Therefore, a child born to an enslaved mother was automatically a slave, even if the child’s father was a free “White” man. By breeding their slaves, plantation owners could increase their wealth without economic investment. Monopoly capitalism at its finest. Related: Trump, Iran and the New Middle East Power Shift As European societies increasingly recognized that human slavery was entirely inconsistent with Christianity, and as Latin American colonies threw off French and Spanish colonial rule (Haiti in 1804 and Mexico in 1821), the United States doubled down on human slavery. The plantation economy of the American South was the greatest source of income for the new nation. And it depended entirely on slave labor. Although sermons and treatises defended human slavery as beneficial and “Christian,” more and more voices were raised in support of abolition. Slave owners and the governments that depended on slavery-generated income passed laws making it illegal to teach slaves to read, write, and do arithmetic. Enslaved Christian preachers were criminalized, with increasingly severe restrictions imposed after preachers like Nat Turner encouraged freedom in the name of Christianity. Leading up to the American Civil War, there was no longer any pretense. Race-based human slavery was an economic engine. In 1845, Southern plantation owners who were members of the Baptist Church in America broke away from the main Baptist organization and founded the Southern Baptist Convention (SBC). The two groups’ theology remained the same, with the exception that the SBC proclaimed that “Black” people were created inferior by God and were destined to exist in eternal servitude to the White master race. The creation of the SBC was an entirely economic move, with no pretense of any scientific basis. It was simply an announcement by wealthy plantation owners that their economic interests mandated the creation of their own new religion, rejecting the Christian teachings of both Catholic and Protestant churches around the world. The same logic underlay the creation of the Klan and all Jim Crow laws. But the economic interests were not specific to race. The successes of the labor movement in the first decades of the 20th century were limited by efforts to convince White workers to see “Black” and “Latin” workers as economic enemies. The interest was not racial separation but dissension between visibly identifiable groups of workers, keeping them from forming stronger unions that might demand bigger pieces of the industrial pie. Historians of the late 18th and early 19th centuries point to identical efforts by American diplomats negotiating with Native American tribes. While numerous diplomats recorded Native American efforts to persuade tribes to put aside their differences and consolidate their efforts to resist land takeovers in the Ohio Valley and other areas southeast of the Mississippi River, the record of treaties made and then broken consistently shows diplomats’ efforts to deal with individual tribes rather than groups (unions?) of tribes. After World War II, which followed the great economic democratizing successes of the New Deal, the Civil Rights Movement gained momentum. While many of today’s “progressives” and “revolutionaries” spout stock “Marxist” phraseology against religion, the Civil Rights Movement did what labor unions had failed to do. Churches of various denominations encouraged the involvement of all people in the struggle. Fundamentalists who believed that Catholics sided with Satan and that Jews killed Jesus agreed to work with Catholics and Jews to end segregation. Looking at innumerable civil rights activities, we focus on a few heroic women, such as Rosa Parks and Mamie Till-Mobley. The movement was built on the labor of women before there was a Women’s Movement. It was built on the work of nuns, the efforts of women working in Jewish congregations and Protestant churches, women performers spreading messages of freedom, and the work of women who, decades earlier, had developed tactics and messages for women’s suffrage. Related: From Bull Connor to ICE: The Return of State-Sanctioned Violence The Women’s Movement met as much resistance as the Labor Movement had, albeit with less overt violence, from the same forces that, in the 1930s, 1950s, and the 1960s, had opposed every other effort to get working people to see themselves first as working people with common interests, rather than as people with different skin tones, national and religious backgrounds, or differently formed eyelids. In a rejection, even a denial, of science, firefighters and police officers were encouraged to resist the inclusion of women in their “male” professions. And the same foolishness continues today as the nation’s secretary of defense rails that women can’t perform in leadership roles or in combat, even as every modern nation around the world has successfully integrated women into its war machine. The same secretary, for the same divide-and-conquer reasons, is denying qualified “Black” and “Brown” men promotions and positions of authority. It’s easy to see why corporations that thrive on low-paid labor and those that suck down tax dollars for unproven weaponry want to promote divisive thinking. Billions of dollars are at stake in every budget year. No one wants to give money to workers instead of allocating it to management bonuses and shareholder dividends. But it is our tax money. It is our consumer money. Discrimination against Asians, Blacks, Latinos, and Native Americans has never been about race. It has been about economic advantages. Cheap Chinese and Irish laborers were both imported to build our railroads. Both were called “inferior,” while the corporations that imported them really meant “cheaper.” There were times when Eastern Europeans and Southern Europeans were imported as cheaper and supposedly “inferior” workers. Hungarians and other Eastern Europeans (collectively disparaged as “Hunkies”) filled steel mills. Italians (“Wops”) filled cheap factory and agricultural jobs. The use of derogatory nicknames helped—and continues to help—maintain their categorization as separate from and inferior to “real Americans.” In the 1640 Virginia case involving John Punch, racial distinctions that had no meaning for the defendants were beneficial to businessmen. Three men, all indentured to Hugh Glyn, ran away from Virginia but were captured in Maryland. They were punished for fleeing from indentured servitude. John Punch was a “Black” servant. The two runaways with him were “White.” The two White runaways were sentenced to longer periods of indenture. John Punch was sentenced to lifetime servitude. Racism is not a natural phenomenon. Running away from slavery was a regular feature of life in the American colonies. And although Africans generally had darker skin tones than Native Americans, runaway slaves were often accepted and adopted into Native American clans and families. Related: Privatize the Profits, Socialize the Costs But racism can be learned. As colonial intrusion shrank Native American communities, those communities tried to find ways to resist, fight back, and reclaim lands taken from them by settlers moving west from the growing United States. The Cherokee Nation tried to model its government on that of the United States, developing its own written language, writing a constitution, and forming a bicameral legislature and a judiciary independent of executive functions. The Cherokees had prospered economically. They built plantations and exported cotton and other crops to the United States. They worked their plantations with slave labor, even while incorporating free “Black” people into Cherokee families and communities. But when the Cherokee Constitution was adopted in 1827, it explicitly disenfranchised “Black” people, including the “Black”-fathered children of Cherokee women. To succeed in business relations with their dominant neighbor, Cherokees learned to adopt American racism after having been welcoming to “Black” people fleeing slavery for more than two centuries. Similarly, both French and Spanish legal systems recognized property ownership and legal personhood for women. Women could buy, inherit, manage, and sell their own property. But when the United States took over French and Spanish territories, it imposed English “common law,” under which a woman’s property became her husband’s and her legal personhood was subsumed into his. There were no biological or other scientific reasons for this. It was simply a feudal system that concentrated financial control in limited hands. The experiences of indentured servants, Native Americans abandoning traditional societal inclusiveness, workers trying to organize, and women trying to live in their respective societies each teach us that scientific realities can be overcome by social training. The Labor Movement, Civil Rights Movement, Women’s Rights Movement, and Gay Rights Movement all teach us that training can move societies away from artificial bigotries. The forces of economic self-interest will always push divisiveness. It is in their interest to increase conflict and pit their workers and customers against each other. The fear of losing a job opportunity to another applicant is similar to the fear of losing the last Cabbage Patch doll to another customer in the holiday rush. Pushing fear as a marketing technique to increase profit is natural. It is as old as competing preachers proclaiming that they each have access to the only eternal truths. But let us not solely blame businessmen and the defenders of social “traditions.” As the October Left Coast Forum also showed us, “leftist” organizations have their own traditions of divisive thinking. Marxists point out the dogmatic purity of Leninists, who disdain backsliders and people who differ over points of dogma. And “everybody” hates the Trotskyites. It is easy to find “progressives” who are eager to attack their allies over details of policies on which they nominally agree. “Race” is one of those policies. For many progressives, accepting the traditional, conservative definition that racial distinctions exist is their natural starting point. After all, they have learned all their lives that race exists and that race matters. They “know” that it’s real because they’ve experienced its effects all their lives. Changing that thinking will not stop those who benefit from racism from continuing to practice it, continuing to promote it, and continuing to benefit from it. But changing the training can, has, and will disrupt the efforts of bigots and profiteers and move society toward further abandoning the artifices created by colonial businessmen in the early 17th century. The Cherokee National Constitution of 1827 didn’t prevent the forced military removal of the Cherokee Nation from its land under Andrew Jackson. But years later, the Cherokee removed the explicitly racist, exclusionary language. If those whom our Founding Fathers called “the savage Indians” could learn to adopt and then abandon artificial constructs, shouldn’t we “superior” modern people be able to learn at least as well? Related: AI, the Bible, and the Battle Over Who Controls Knowledge President Obama delivered a speech on his racial position and got himself elected president of the United States. He delivered the long-overdue beginnings of a national healthcare program, which led to his condemnation by both racist, pro-business healthcare backers and “progressives” who thought he didn’t deliver enough, despite the strident and staunch opposition embodied in Mitch McConnell’s “one-term president” decree. The 16th Amendment moved the needle. It didn’t make our tax system fair, just fairer. The 19th Amendment gave women the vote. It didn’t make all women vote sensibly, any more than male suffrage makes MAGA men vote sensibly. The failure of the Equal Rights Amendment did not stop the development of the Women’s Movement or the great (if still inadequate) strides toward equality for women. The same can and must be said of race. Race is an artificial construct, created and maintained for the benefit of economically controlling interests. It has no objective reality. But it enjoys widespread belief and acceptance. A proper progressive response to racial discrimination in our society is not to continue to accept it as “reality” but rather to begin to attack the fake construct itself and work to rob it of its social acceptance. Exploiting racial themes for fundraising and political leverage is effective. We have increasingly diverse representation at all levels of government. People seeking government services encounter government employees from an increasingly broad range of ethnicities, religions, and national origins, all to the benefit of society. Exposing pernicious racism when it presents itself remains a necessary part of the process. It leads to progress. We need to find new language for talking about “race”—new language that is not grounded in acceptance of conservative and business-centered divisiveness, definitions, and terminology. New language that can speak both to progressives and to those who are coming to see that their support for the Donald and for corporate oligarchy was misplaced and self-injuring. It won’t be easy, but new language can help us develop a new construct about “race,” a new understanding that it isn’t real. Working out new language will be messy, as all important social progress is. We learned in the early 20th century to “dial” our telephones. How many of today’s children “dial” their cell phones without any idea of what the term even means? What verb will emerge to refer to the process of mechanical arms reaching out to catch descending rocket ships, replacing the long sentence used by SpaceX to describe its new process of handling returning spaceships? Race itself was once a new term. François Bernier, a French physician, proposed dividing humans into four races back in 1684, 44 years after John Punch was sentenced to lifetime servitude. Ignoring the fact that it took some years for Dr. Bernier’s idea to spread widely, 342 years is long enough for his faulty concept to be abandoned. But it should take many, many fewer years to convince Americans to abandon it, as so much of the rest of civilization has. Related: Young Blood Isn’t Enough—and Neither Is Experience The midterm elections were a wake-up call, showing that American voters are frustrated and open to change. But open to what change? Republicans, with their embrace of the Donald’s appointment of Stephen Miller and their defense of Pete Hegseth, have shown their intractability. What of progressives? Can they rethink their commitment to conservative, economically driven definitions of race? Can they meet the voters’ challenge to change old, stale, economically devastating definitions and assumptions? Can they learn to abandon false but profitable language for a new construct—a world that denies the false construct?

articles.title: Failed Housing System
articles.author: Dick Platkin
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Los Angeles has a new mayor, Nithya Raman, who will soon be sworn into her four year mayoral term. Can we assume things will then improve, especially regarding the homeless and overcrowded? In a word, NO. This is why. Nithya Raman presented a reduction in the number of homeless people as a success in her fourth Council District, but this statistic has two problems. First, the process which creates widespread and increasing homeless not only remains, but is increasing. Second, her actions did not include the overcrowded, who number over a million in the Los Angeles region. Together, the increasing homeless and overcrowded numbers reveal the inherent problems her and other elected officials face in making sure all Angelenos have an adequate place to live. The reason is not a shortage of vacant apartments or even houses. For example in my older Los Angeles neighborhood, near Wilshire Boulevard and the new D subway line , there is a vacant apartment on nearly every block. The homeless and overcrowded would gladly move into these vacant apartments if they could afford them. But they cannot come up with the first month’s rent, damage deposit, and last month’s rent. If they had enough savings, they would be able to rent a vacant apartment, but they can’t afford to. The barrier is not supply, but the dire financial situation of the homeless and overcrowded. Is there a solution this problem? Of course there is, but it is no longer available. The answer is public housing, a signature feature of the New Deal. These programs began in the mid-1930’s and ended in the early 1970’s, when the Nixon administration (1968 – 1973), with the eventual support of Congressional Democrats, ended these HUD housing programs. Nevertheless, some public housing survives in the United States as older housing that has not yet been shut down to make way for private sector housing. In Los Angeles, for example, there still is available public housing, but it is around 50 or more years old. What is now available had to be built before 1970. Related: Over-crowded Homes in LA County and How to Help Them In some cities, like Seattle, most public housing projects, such as Holly Park, have been demolished and replaced with private sector housing. In Los Angeles, a few public housing projects survive, but they are still hanging on until they too give way to private sector housing. The solution: A few European countries, like Austria and Finland, still have publicly built and operated housing, so we know that it is still possible. But public housing is not in the cards for the USA. Even Bernie Sanders, the 85 year old Independent Senator from Vermont, no longer proposes HUD (Dept. of Urban Affairs) public housing on his website . Related: Living in Cars: LA's Hidden Homelessness Crisis Unfortunately without the resurrection of public housing in this country, we will witness increasing levels of homelessness and overcrowding, like the current situation in Los Angeles. Knowing that public housing programs offer a viable alternative give us something to propose to the new Democratic majorities in the Senate and the House. My advice to you is not to hold your breath because, however, the Democratic politicians in DC, like the new Mayor in LA, are not about to call for a return of HUD public housing programs.

articles.title: Thanksgiving Myth
articles.author: Jasmyne Cannick
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. I know it's unpopular to talk about certain things on Thanksgiving because apparently we're supposed to suspend our critical thinking for the day in the interest of everybody's comfort. But I'm Gen X, our motto continues to be fuck your feelings, and at my big age, other people's discomfort is not a sufficient reason for me to shut up. If what I'm about to say is going to interfere with your enjoyment of today's festivities, exercise your God-given ability to keep scrolling. I'm not serving dinner, and reading this ain't mandatory. That said… The thing about being a Gen X woman is that the older I get and the more I learn about this country, past and present, the more I find myself questioning some of the shit we grew up doing simply because that’s what everybody else was doing. Thanksgiving is one of those things. We grew up tracing our hands to make turkeys while America conveniently left the stolen land, broken treaties, genocide and forced displacement of Indigenous people out of the lesson plan. Apparently, that part didn’t fit on the bulletin board. America has perfected the art of committing atrocities, rewriting the history, giving itself a federal holiday and throwing in a mattress sale. And please spare me the lecture about Thanksgiving being about gratitude. Gratitude is available 365 days a year, 366 during a leap year. It does not require a federally designated Thursday, a dead bird or a historically questionable origin story. Related: Los Angeles Mayor’s Race: When Progressive Branding Replaces Progressive Governing As a Black woman, I cannot demand that America reckon with what it did to my people while conveniently overlooking what it did to Indigenous people because somebody’s auntie makes exceptional dressing. My commitment to justice is not contingent upon the menu and I’m not about to play intellectually incompetent for the sake of a plate of dressing. My solidarity with other oppressed people shouldn’t go on hiatus because it’s the fourth Thursday in November. And quiet as it’s kept, America is still very much in the business of deciding whose humanity matters and whose doesn’t. Today, so many people will pass human beings splayed across the concrete, sleeping in tents and living on the streets, on their way to somebody’s house to sit around a table and talk about how thankful and blessed they are. Some of those same people will spend tomorrow complaining about the homeless people in their neighborhood. Make that shit make sense. You’re thankful for the roof over your head but resentful of the person who doesn’t have one. Thankful for the food on your table but offended by the person asking for something to eat. But by all means, somebody bless the food. At some point, what we profess to believe has to inform how we actually live. Otherwise, we’re just performing consciousness when it’s convenient. I’m Gen X. I’m old enough to understand that consistency requires sacrifice and that sometimes standing on your principles means sitting out some shit you actually enjoy. Related: The Real Democratic Debate Begins in Los Angeles Listen, I’m not telling anybody what to do with their Thursday. I’m grown and presumably so are you. But I refuse to be more committed to the traditions of my childhood than I am to the convictions of my adulthood. I don’t need a federal holiday to be thankful. I don’t need to participate in America’s historical revisionism to spend time with people I love. And I damn sure don’t need permission from anybody to stop celebrating something that no longer aligns with my beliefs. I can be grateful without celebrating a mythology that sanitizes the suffering of Indigenous people. And I can express that gratitude by giving a damn about the people suffering right outside my door today. Some of us have outgrown Thanksgiving. Not the food. The bullshit. And contrary to popular belief, macaroni and cheese can legally be made any day of the year. Jasmyne's Substack

articles.title: Illusion of Peace
articles.author: Ramzy Baroud
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. An established maxim of Islamic jurisprudence, known in Arabic as ma buniya ‘ala batil fa-huwa batil , holds that “what is built upon falsehood is itself false.” A related jurisprudential principle maintains that “if the foundation is invalid, what follows from it is also invalid.” Few places in the world today illustrate the enduring relevance of this wisdom more starkly than Gaza. Consider the political framework imposed on Gaza in the name of peace. We continue to speak of a ceasefire, of US President Donald Trump’s Gaza plan, and of UN Security Council Resolution 2803, adopted on November 17, 2025, which endorsed the plan and lent international legitimacy to the political arrangements that were supposed to follow. Yet, in reality, there is no functioning political arrangement, no meaningful transformation of conditions on the ground, and certainly no ceasefire worthy of the name. Related: Zionism, Gaza, and the Battle Over Palestine's History Those who enthusiastically voted for the US-sponsored resolution have yet to acknowledge that they were, at the very least, misled about Washington’s intentions. The organizations and individuals who championed the plan have yet to apologize for their role in deceiving Palestinians, particularly the families of the 1,658 people killed and 6,000 wounded since the so-called ceasefire took effect on October 10, 2025. Until such a moral reckoning takes place, we will continue to inhabit a surreal reality in which George Orwell’s dystopian dictum, “War is peace,” has become the governing language of international diplomacy. Consider Israel’s latest invasion of central Gaza. On November 18, Israeli tanks and bulldozers advanced beyond the so-called yellow line into areas designated as blocks 660, 661 and 666, northeast of Nuseirat refugee camp and northwest of Al-Bureij. Under the familiar pretext of a ‘security’ operation, Israeli forces shelled residential neighborhoods, closed sections of Salah al-Din Road and forced thousands of Palestinians to flee yet again. On that same day, Gaza’s Health Ministry reported seven deaths and 15 injuries over the preceding 24 hours. These were merely the latest additions to an almost uninterrupted daily tally of Palestinians killed and wounded since the supposed cessation of hostilities. The invasion came as Gaza was still reeling from devastating floods that began on November 6. According to Palestinian authorities, at least 70,000 tents sheltering displaced families were flooded, while UN assessments documented damage to more than 40,000 shelters, including over 9,000 rendered uninhabitable. The floods also claimed lives, including children, leaving thousands of families exposed to cold, rain and further displacement. Thus, even as Palestinians are told that the war has ended, they continue to die from Israeli bombardment, collapsing buildings, contaminated water and the consequences of a devastated infrastructure. Some analysts who examined the latest Israeli invasion have offered various explanations for Netanyahu’s renewed onslaught. Some suggest that he is attempting to provoke a wider confrontation to pressure his political rivals into joining a unity government. Others argue that he is seeking to distract from his mounting domestic political troubles, or that the invasion represents a compromise between launching another war against Iran and taking no military action at all. Related: The Iran War, Israel Aid, and the Political Fallout for Trump These explanations, however plausible, make not an iota of difference to Palestinians, who continue to endure a genocide that never truly stopped, regardless of how insistently the international community invokes the word “ceasefire.” Hamas and other Palestinian resistance groups continue to call upon the so-called Board of Peace and the agreement’s guarantors to fulfill their obligations, particularly regarding the unrestricted entry of humanitarian aid. According to Gaza’s Government Media Office, only 79,585 aid trucks had entered the Strip by November 16, compared with the 240,600 stipulated under the agreement. This represents a compliance rate of barely 33 percent. But Palestinian resistance groups also face the limits of their strategic patience. While their immediate priority remains protecting Gaza’s population and ensuring the entry of essential supplies and reconstruction materials, they cannot indefinitely allow Israel to resume open warfare without resistance. The question, therefore, is how much longer that strategic patience can endure before the entire arrangement unravels. Meanwhile, Gaza is condemned to a prolonged catastrophe: a genocide sustained at a lower intensity, punctuated by periodic massacres, compounded by preventable deaths from disease, contaminated water, exposure and flooding, all while the fiction of a functioning ceasefire is meticulously preserved. What is urgently needed is political accountability from those who were either deceived by, or willingly endorsed, the Gaza plan. Rather than delivering genuine peace, the arrangement has served Israeli and US objectives by buying time to pursue the disarmament of Palestinian resistance, while leaving Gaza’s population exposed to continued military attacks, deprivation and the threat of further displacement. Related: Palestinians Beat Israel's Political System at Its Own Game Equally necessary is moral accountability from UN officials and other international figures who defended the US resolution as a genuine foundation for lasting peace, despite the absence of credible mechanisms capable of compelling Israel to honor its commitments. Such accountability will not emerge spontaneously. It must be demanded. Indeed, it must be exacted. Perhaps one of the most consequential successes of the Trump-Netanyahu ceasefire scheme has been its ability to diminish the momentum of international solidarity with Gaza. Even governments that profess sympathy for Palestinians have embraced the language of a truce, using the appearance of diplomatic progress to justify their own inaction and discourage renewed mass mobilization among their civil societies. This must change. Otherwise, Israel, emboldened by US support and the complicity of other Western allies, will continue exploiting the illusion of peace until it finds the most opportune moment to unleash another full-scale assault on Gaza, this time with the intention of completing the destruction it began more than three years ago. The Palestine Chronicle

articles.title: Richard Wolff on Becoming an American Marxist
articles.author: Sharon Kyle, Dick Price
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. The best education Richard Wolff got at Harvard, he told us, began when a man knocked on his dorm-room door. Fritz Pappenheim, a scholar who had served the Spanish Republican government during the civil war, had fled to France after Franco’s victory. Wolff’s father, an old friend, helped him get papers to stay in Paris and later a visa to come to the United States. Years later, Pappenheim found a way to repay him. He offered to teach his son to read Marx in German. The arrangement was simple. Every couple of weeks, the Harvard freshman would come over for dinner and French wine. Pappenheim would find Marxist writings on whatever Wolff was studying, and the two would talk through the readings. Wolff could then bring both sets of work to his papers on subjects like the French Revolution and World War I. His professors gave him high marks. They seemed to think the insights were his own, he recalled. For four years, Wolff had two educations running side by side. The one that would shape his life began with an invitation to read what his professors left out. His father would later urge him to stay in school and earn the credentials that, in his view, could protect a young radical. Wolff came to appreciate the advice. Degrees from Harvard, Stanford and Yale gave him room to teach ideas that had once been risky even to discuss at school. That story is part of Question Everything: Professor Richard Wolff on Becoming an American Marxist , a book-length conversation with his former student Ian Seda-Irizarry, now an economics professor at John Jay College. The two started meeting over Zoom during the pandemic, working through Wolff’s family history, his education and the ways his teaching and political work shaped each other. Democracy at Work announced a December 7 release. Related: Beyond Trump: Why Democrats Need a New New Deal for Working Americans Who gets the fruits of the labor? When we asked Wolff where a Marxist starts in looking at any economy, he began with a question anybody who has held a job can ask. “Who gets the fruits of the labor of the people doing work?” Consider the example he gave us. A blouse manufacturer offers you $25 an hour. The company expects your work to add more than $25 an hour in value, whether you help make more blouses or improve the ones it sells. In Wolff’s explanation of Marx, the difference between the value workers add and what they receive in wages is the surplus. Workers produce it. Owners decide how to use it. The money can go toward expanding the business, buying new equipment or rewarding investors. What interests Wolff is who gets to make those decisions. The people who put in the hours have to live on their wages, while the people who control the surplus can use it to increase their wealth and extend their influence. That’s where workplace democracy comes in. Wolff asked us to imagine a restaurant or factory run on the principle of one worker, one vote. The people who do the work would decide together what to produce, what technology to use, where to operate and how to distribute what’s left after paying the bills. In a restaurant, that might mean deciding together whether to replace aging equipment, raise pay or put money aside for a slow season. The people who live with those decisions would have a vote in making them. Related: China and the US: Meeting Is Good, Agreement Is Better How racial division creates a foothold Sharon asked what happens when politicians persuade the public that a racialized group deserves fewer rights or less protection. Can elites use that acceptance as a foothold to hold down wages, limit political participation and accumulate more power? Wolff answered with the example of an undocumented construction worker. A boss can withhold a paycheck knowing that the worker may be afraid to report the theft for fear of deportation. The boss gains leverage from that fear. Then politicians can encourage other workers, who are also struggling to get by, to blame immigrants for low wages or deteriorating public services. The employer’s power gets less scrutiny, and people who might have made common cause are encouraged to see each other as the problem. Wolff pointed to Donald Trump’s use of the word “invasion” for migration across the southern border. Describing people who have left their homes and families as an invading army makes it easier for the public to accept their mistreatment. For Sharon, this is where the foothold matters. Once the public accepts weaker protections for one group, employers can turn that vulnerability into leverage at work, and political leaders can use the divisions it creates to make a broader challenge to their power harder to mount. The people targeted bear the immediate harm. The division weakens the bargaining position of workers who might otherwise stand together. For Wolff, the subject is personal. His parents fled Europe, and members of both sides of his family were killed in the Holocaust. In the United States, his father’s credentials as a lawyer and judge went unrecognized. The Quakers helped him find work, and by the time Richard was born in Youngstown, Ohio, his father was supplementing his teaching income by pushing a wheelbarrow at Youngstown Sheet and Tube. Richard grew up speaking German and some French and learned English when he went to kindergarten. Related: From Welfare State to Warfare State: Europe’s Dangerous Turn What a fight for reform can teach Dick asked how incremental reforms might add up to structural change, taking New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani as an example. Wolff pointed to stronger rent protections and city-run grocery stores in underserved neighborhoods as reforms that could improve people’s lives. He was equally interested in what happens when people organize for those changes and encounter the limits of what officials can deliver. Both Sharon and Wolff came back to campaign finance. An elected official who depends on wealthy donors has to consider what those donors will do when a policy threatens their interests. Wolff saw a different source of political power in Mamdani’s campaign. People gave $10 or $20, sometimes more than once, and volunteers kept showing up at voters’ doors. Canvassers knocked at Wolff’s own apartment four times, he recalled. Nobody came by for any other candidate. Winning an election gives that kind of organization a chance to change policy. The fights that follow can show people where power still sits and what they would have to organize to change. For Wolff, that is how a campaign over rents or groceries can lead to a larger fight about who makes the decisions that shape a city. Wolff told us that his father once asked him to help take books about socialism off the family shelves. They put them into boxes in the basement and covered the boxes with blankets. His father was curious about those ideas and afraid of what could happen if a neighbor saw them. Years later, Pappenheim put some of those ideas back within reach. Wolff has spent his career doing the same for students and for listeners of Economic Update . As he put it to us, “Being a teacher made me a better political activist.” He credits his activism with making him a better teacher, too. The question his teaching leaves with us is one we can take into a workplace, an election or a fight over rents. Who gets to decide, and what would it take for the people who live with the decision to have a say?

articles.title: Baby Kohen Wiley
articles.author: Melina Abdullah
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Hunter Foster has the blood of an innocent baby on his hands, as does the entire Senatobia police department. On June 14, the former sergeant shot into a car that was attempting to leave a Walmart parking lot, stealing the life of one-year-old Kohen Wiley, who was being held in his young mother’s arms. Four months later, Mississippi Attorney General Lynn Fitch deemed this horrific killing “justified.” Just as fervently as I pray that Baby Kohen’s soul finds rest, just as fervently as I pray that his parents’ hearts are stitched back together, I also pray that Foster and Fitch face God’s wrath. I pray that they suffer as they have caused such deep suffering. I pray that they never have a moment’s peace, that they are thrust to the depths of hell, and that their entire lineages be cursed. As a woman of deep faith, I pray. And “faith without works is dead.” As servants of God, we are compelled to also work towards the justice for which we pray. We must demand that Hunter Foster face prison and poverty, denied work, placed behind bars, and shunned by the world. Instead of throwing her hat in the ring for Mississippi governor, Lynn Fitch must be disbarred, her family plantation seized, and every penny of wealth that she hoards paid out in reparations to Kohen’s family and the generations of stolen and enslaved Black people from which her bloodline enriched themselves. Related: In the Name of Nolan Wells: A Christian Call for Truth, Faith, and Justice We work towards systemic change too. Senatobia police should be defunded, its resources rerouted to jobs and education programs that would provide Baby Kohen’s mother a college education, his father a living wage, and a universal basic income to the 27% of Senatobians who currently live in poverty. Systemic transformation must reach be far-reaching. White-supremacist-capitalism must be toppled. Baby Kohen’s murder was at the behest of Walmart. Initial reports were that police were greenlit to kill because the baby’s mother and her friend had stolen a pack of diapers. (They had not.) Like John Crawford was deemed dangerous and killed by police for holding store merchandise in the aisles of a Walmart in Beavercreek, Ohio. Like the police shooting of Steven Taylor came because his mental health crisis disturbed the flow of capital inside a Walmart near Oakland, California. In each case, Walmart either called or covered for police. There is not a case on record, where the trillion-dollar company has condemned police violence in their stores or anywhere nor have they cooperated with families of those killed by cops. Cops and capitalism are extensions of one another, with the primary function of policing being to protect corporate profit. Related: Black Lives Matter LA Has 10 Demands for Mayor-Elect Nithya Raman Like we must hold Hunter Foster, Lynn Fitch, policing, and the entire criminal legal system accountable, so, too, must we hold Walmart and the white-supremacist-capitalism accountable. For the last 11 years, Black Lives Matter Grassroots has called for the deliberate use of our collective economic power, especially during the holidays. We launched Black Xmas in the name of John Crawford, employing three core tenets: BUILD BLACK – Invest dollars in Black-led, Black serving organizations to grow our collective power. BUY BLACK – When we must buy, buy from Black businesses that benefit Black community. BANK BLACK – Move funds out of white-owned banks, many of which made their initial fortunes from chattel slavery and continued to exploit Black people through redlining, predatory lending, and more. To support these efforts, Black Lives Matter Grassroots launched blackxmas.org , a source for Black economic empowerment, including hundreds of Black-owned businesses sorted by type, allowing easy searches. Black Lives Matter-Los Angeles goes even further, posting a Black-owned business every day during Black Xmas season, from Black Friday (Nov. 27) until New Year’s Day. As we work to develop Black cooperative economic structures, this year we are asking folks to make a special commitment to boycott Walmart. We initiated a pledge at tinyurl.com/BoycottWalmartNow and plan to engage in community conversations in Walmart parking lots throughout the season. Walmart is the very worst of the worst and represents the whole of a white-supremacist-capitalist structure that routinely steals Black life. Baby Kohen would be two-years-old now. His parents and grandparents imagine themselves showering him with Christmas gifts. Instead, they will visit his gravesite. Related: Representation Is Not Liberation: Why I Vote My Values, Not My Loyalties The theft of this baby’s life must not go unanswered. It must not rest with the determination of an Attorney General who still holds her family plantation, a cop embroiled in decades of documented racist violence, a police department overrun by rabid racists, or a corporation that makes Black death a routine part of their business. People who move righteously and courageously can change the trajectory of the economy and the world. In the name of Baby Kohen Wiley. In the name of John Crawford. In the name of Steven Taylor. And in honor of all of our people. The Los Angeles Sentinel

articles.title: GTA VI Takes Capitalism Seriously
articles.author: Tim Brinkhof
articles.content: In the first twenty-odd hours of playing Grand Theft Auto VI , the long-awaited latest installment in developer Rockstar’s open-world simulations of contemporary America, I chased a hovercraft with a helicopter, raced Jet Skis around a superyacht, and shot my way out of a hospital in a wheelchair — though not before spending all my stolen cash on medical bills. I also fixed the leaky roof of my apartment, bought flowers for my incarcerated girlfriend when I learned she was about to be let out on parole, and wiped an unexpected tear from my eye as I watched her jump into the arms of a friend who — for a moment — seemed to be on the brink of tears herself. The blockbuster game’s more slice-of-life-oriented gameplay and sentimental, relationship-focused story are relatively new additions to this franchise, especially compared to the detached and bombastic satire of its immediate predecessor. But while journalists have given GTA VI perfect or near-perfect reviews, many right-wing gamers are outraged. To audiences of millions, they complain that Rockstar has replaced the testosterone-fueled wish fulfillment of previous games with what pro-MAGA streamer Zack Hoyt (Asmongold) called a “cuck simulator” and, by doing so, become the latest company in this once exclusively and unapologetically masculine industry to go woke. Responding to this outrage, progressives like Hasan Piker were quick to point out that — actually — the franchise has always been woke. I agree but also believe that such responses shut the door on another, equally interesting discussion. By focusing on GTA VI ’s portrayal of masculinity, public discourse has yet to appreciate how the game engages with another topic central to its identity: capitalism. In line with today’s circumstances, Rockstar has ditched the more overtly comedic parodies of games past, opting instead to portray the everyday struggles of its working-class protagonists in a more serious and sympathetic light. As a result, the gap between its world and the real one has never been smaller. A Franchise Built on Parody Grand Theft Auto became both famous and infamous for the way it enabled and even encouraged its (often young) players to engage in violent, antisocial behavior, from stealing cars and robbing stores to creatively and indiscriminately murdering the AI-generated NPCs — non-player characters — that populate the franchise’s increasingly lifelike cities. What recurring moral panics around the corruptive influence of these games never seemed to grasp, though, is that the developers deliberately matched this gameplay with stories that explored how violence isn’t just random or personal but integral to the structure and functioning of neoliberal society. In each game, the violence committed by its usually marginalized main characters is placed in favorable contrast with the violence committed by their cop, politician, and billionaire opponents. The ensuing conflicts show that the line separating legal from illegal is mostly arbitrary, and wealth impossible to accumulate without a willingness to hurt others. Every new installment approaches this conceit from a slightly different angle. Inspired by hood films and hip-hop, GTA: San Andreas (2004) is steeped in black street culture, while GTA IV (2008) tells the story of an immigrant who comes to Rockstar’s version of New York in search of a better life, only to find things almost as bad as where he came from. While GTA IV is remembered for having a darker, more cinematic tone, both games were fundamentally parodies, critiquing reality by exaggerating it to such a degree that — despite their ever-increasing immersiveness — there always remained a distance between player and player-character. This approach reached its undisputed zenith with GTA V (2013), whose unprecedentedly interactive open world went hand in hand with Rockstar’s most comedic, absurd, and cynical story yet. One of its three protagonists, an unhinged maniac, was specifically designed to serve as a superconductor for the audience’s ability to create carnage and chaos but offered little in the way of reflection. As with The Wolf of Wall Street , released the same year, the game’s excesses were intended to nauseate. Instead they mostly proved either addictive or desensitizing. From Satire to Sincerity The over-the-top, larger-than-life energy that was everywhere present in GTA V can still be found in its sequel, only it is now relegated to a supporting role. One side character — an erratic drug runner — quickly gets the player into trouble when he starts a turf war with swampland rednecks. His actions lead to some exciting and explosive early missions, but unlike in GTA V , they are not without consequence. Toward the end of the game’s opening act, this emblem of the franchise’s more carefree and lighthearted legacy is — spoiler alert — literally fed to the pigs. It’s a subtextual warning for the rest of the game, as well as the setup for a genuinely touching moment of mourning for a death that previous games would have simply laughed off. GTA V was developed during the optimism and relative stability of the Obama administrations, when — for many middle-class Americans — the perils of capitalism were far enough away to be mostly spiritual rather than material, manifesting in a vague desire for meaning and authenticity. GTA VI ’s thirteen-year-long development, by contrast, spanned both Donald Trump terms: a period during which the struggles of its characters — their inability to find stable employment, unfair treatment by institutions, and lack of upward mobility — have become more relatable than ever, imbuing them with a gravity and intimacy they did not possess before. GTA VI ’s move from satire to sincerity corresponds with a broader trend in mass media. As the hosts of the Critics at Large podcast at The New Yorker discussed in an episode released in April, more and more of today’s mainstream entertainment — from Hollywood films to reality TV shows — is shedding the trademark cynicism and irony of postmodernism in favor of a post-postmodern embrace of earnestness and empathy. Not just because, in times as precarious as now, escapism is a luxury that people can no longer afford, but also because we turn to art to feel emotions that regular life doesn’t readily provide. A New Front in the Culture War GTA VI is not the first game to be turned into a major battleground of the culture wars. Another long-standing franchise, God of War , about a Spartan general who fights and kills gods, has likewise angered conservatives for reinventing its nihilistically sadistic protagonist as a caring father and thereby distancing itself from the gratuitous violence and sex appeal of older games. Rockstar, too, has chosen reformation. Not simply for the sake of profit, but also because its developers realize that GTA bears great responsibility for creating the persistent notion that games are and should remain a space where toxic masculinity and political incorrectness are perfectly okay. Studying the right-wing response to GTA VI helps us understand how culture war controversies around media properties are shaped by, and in turn shape, politics. Many criticisms of the game verge on the conspiratorial, with content creators and commentators believing gaming journalists are in Rockstar’s pocket, while Rockstar itself is brainwashing gamers on behalf of the woke elite. At the same time, they also echo populist and fascist narratives of nostalgia and decline: the franchise’s original creators have been pushed out by foreign agents and corrupted GTA from the inside, feeding a longing for a lost golden age of originality and excellence. Though currently dismissed as fringe, the reactionary backlash to GTA VI — the single biggest media event in recent memory — could well fuel a conservative resurgence in the future. At the same time, if the game is truly the cultural barometer that everyone says it is, it also gives plenty of reason to be hopeful. Reflecting, and to some extent perhaps even explaining, recent left-wing electoral victories, Rockstar’s vision of the country is one in which the oppressed choose solidarity and compassion over despair or alienation, and the desire for a better, more equitable future is worth taking seriously. articles.title: The Socialist History Behind Thanksgiving’s Most Iconic Image
articles.author: Liza Featherstone
articles.content: An older woman, still wearing her apron from all her work in the kitchen, brings a large turkey to a table set with cranberry sauce and fruit and full of family, friends, and neighbors, who are smiling, talking, enjoying one another’s company. Her husband stands beside her at the head of the table, surveying the scene with pride. The 1943 Norman Rockwell oil painting has become perhaps the most iconic and ubiquitous image of Thanksgiving in our modern era. It looks like a classic piece of kitschy, complacent Americana. Yet the image has a surprising political history. With so many in America going hungry this year, it’s a good time to remember that the painting was commissioned in honor of Franklin Delano Roosevelt’s bold call for “Freedom from Want” and released with a much bolder critique of New Deal America for failing to deliver that freedom to everyone. “Freedom from Want” was one of the “Four Freedoms,” values set forth in FDR’s 1941 message to Congress on the need for continued US involvement in World War II, which the US would officially enter eleven months later. In our post–Ronald Reagan world, the very idea sounds revolutionary, especially since FDR said he was describing “the kind of world attainable in our own time and generation.” He argued the entire project of America’s domestic order was an ongoing “peaceful revolution.” The Four Freedoms speech didn’t make much of an impression on the American public when FDR first delivered it. Two years later, the war underway, The Saturday Evening Post commissioned Rockwell to illustrate each of the Four Freedoms, and the artist delivered this image of an abundant Thanksgiving feast to represent “Freedom from Want.” Along with the illustrations, the Post assigned essays to accompany them. “Freedom from Want” was assigned to Carlos Bulosan, a Filipino socialist activist, trade unionist, and writer. Bulosan was born in the Philippines to a peasant family, did not receive a formal education beyond third grade, and grew up picking coconuts and selling them to wholesalers to pay his older brothers’ school fees. He came to the United States at seventeen and worked in a fish cannery in Alaska, eventually becoming organizer and an elected official with the longshoreman’s union. In Washington and California, he worked as a dishwasher, a farm laborer, and in other low-wage jobs. Despite his life’s hardships, he spent many hours in public libraries. Once, during a two-year battle with tuberculosis, he claimed to have read a book a day, including the works of Karl Marx and Walt Whitman. During this same bedridden period in the late 1930s, he began writing, contributing to publications like The New Yorker and Harper’s Bazaar — and The Saturday Evening Post . Bulosan embraced the “Freedom from Want” assignment with a paean to America’s working class, whom he called “the creators of abundance.” His description of that class is rich and expansive: If you want to know what we are, look upon the farms or upon the hard pavements of the city. . . . We cut timbers in Oregon just as the wild flowers blossom in Maine. We are multitudes in Pennsylvania mines, in Alaskan canneries. We are millions from Puget Sound to Florida. In violent factories, crowded tenements, teeming cities. . . . We are factory hands, field hands, mill hands. . . . We are the living dream of dead men. We are the living spirit of free men. He emphasized the working class’s role in driving history forward, seeing that class as the engine of progress, not only through its labor but through its political struggles: We are bleeding where clubs are smashing heads, where bayonets are gleaming. We are fighting where the bullet is crashing upon armorless citizens, where the tear gas is choking unprotected children. Under the lynch trees, amidst hysterical mobs. Bulosan celebrates the progress of such struggles, including the right to organize unions. Yet because of the barbarities and inequalities of capitalism, Americans were still suffering deprivation: We are not really free unless we use what we produce. So long as the fruit of our labor is denied us, so long will want manifest itself in a world of slaves. It is only when we have plenty to eat — plenty of everything — that we begin to understand what freedom means. . . . Our march to freedom is not complete unless want is annihilated. Bulosan’s writing is heavy with disappointment that this vision hadn’t already been realized, emphasizing that the New Deal hadn’t gone far enough. Yet with an end to hunger, he wrote, democracy could be fully realized. He imagined a polity of plenty: When we have enough to eat . . . then we have the time and ability to read and think and discuss things. Then we are not merely living but also becoming a creative part of life. It is only then that we become a growing part of democracy. Rockwell’s painting was originally titled Freedom from Want , though since then, reflecting how this political context has been lost to history, it’s also been called I’ll Be Home for Christmas or simply The Thanksgiving Picture . As many observers have noted, the people around the table are enjoying their time together and are not looking at the turkey; the guests have the luxury of taking the food for granted as they revel in one another’s company. Although Rockwell reportedly worried that his painting didn’t match Bulosan’s radical essay, it’s not hard to see how it does: both envision an America in which the conditions of plentiful comfort support a robust and lively social world. Just about everyone in America would recognize this Thanksgiving painting, but the socialist demand for food abundance that accompanied it has been forgotten. FDR’s Four Freedoms, engraved at the Franklin Delano Roosevelt Memorial in Washington, DC. (Bjorndahl) That demand is more timely than ever. The cost of a typical Thanksgiving feast for ten this year has increased by 6 percent since last year, according to the American Farm Bureau. And if you live in a neighborhood with a food pantry, as I do, you are probably seeing long lines around the block. With the increase in grocery prices and millions thrown off the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) by the Trump administration’s work requirements, food banks are seeing even more hungry people than during the pandemic years, with a dramatic increase in first-time visitors. Damningly, the Trump administration has discontinued the US Department of Agriculture’s annual household food security survey, but the New York Federal Reserve, in a national survey earlier this year, found what it called a “ remarkable ” increase in food insecurity from 2025 to 2026, especially in lower-income households and in households with young children. The New York Fed noted at the time that food insecurity was diminishing Americans’ confidence in the future; it seems certain that this increase in hardship contributed to the recent election results. As so many go hungry in America, even as we elect more leaders in FDR’s tradition, Bulosan’s exhortation to American workers calls to us to push beyond the frame of what seems possible under US capitalism, to make the promises of its democracy real by feeding everyone. “What do we want?” Bulosan asked, invoking the beginning of a timeless protest call and response: We want to share the promises and fruits of American life. We want to be free from fear and hunger. If you want to know what we are — we are marching! articles.title: Going to North Lake
articles.author: Detroit DSA
articles.content: Portraits of those killed by ICE, as well as offerings of food and flowers. All photos by Althea Mukes . By Dianne Feeley On November 1st, supporters of immigrant rights gathered at the North Lake Processing Center–, the largest immigrant prison in the Midwest– with a Day of the Dead ceremony. About 150 activists, including several Michigan DSA chapters ( — Metro Detroit DSA, Greater Lansing DSA, Northwest MI DSA and Huron Valley DSA) — organized the event in coalition with Coalition to Shut the Camps, Movimiento Cosecha, No Detention Centers in Michigan, People’s Assembly and West Michigan Clergy Action. Detention Watch Network, a national network — working to get ICE out of communities, shut down ICE detention centers and redirect the massive ICE funding to meet social needs — loosely coordinated actions at various detention centers across the country and provided a tool kit in English and Spanish. The action was planned for late afternoon, after visitation hours were over for the families of those incarcerated at North Lake. We did not want to jeopardize having the Sunday visits cancelled because of our presence. Metro Detroit reached out to other Michigan DSA chapters and encouraged them to participate. Thanks to our chapter, Metro Detroit sent two vans to North Lake, stopping in Ypsilanti and Lansing to pick up members. Two comrades holding a MDDSA “Solidaridad” banner North Lake Processing Center, operated by GEO Group, has 1800 beds and earns GEO approximately $70 million annually. It is part of a national network of 200 detention centers. While under previous administrations less than 30,000 immigrants were previously detained, the Trump administration plans to more than triple that capacity. Over the last year the Department of Homeland Security has spent more than seven billion dollars to store immigrants in these hell holes and county jails with another two billion earmarked to transport and deport them. Since Trump’s inauguration, more than 60 immigrants have died in these centers. This includes Nenko Stanev Gantchev, 56, who was born in Bulgaria. After nearly a year in declining health at North Lake, he was found “unresponsive” in his cell on December 15, 2025. In addition, ICE has murdered or caused the death of seven people in the streets. Besides the well-known executions of Renee Good and Alex Pretti, others have been trapped and shot in their cars or have attempted to flee. Just a week earlier, on October 24, Mario David Coronado Juárez, 35, was stopped by ICE in Grand Rapids (just an hour south of North Lake) as they searched for someone else. A 35-year-old construction worker, Coronado Juárez, who was sending money home to his family in Guatemala, Coronado Juárez sped away, crashed into a tree and died. Day of the Dead (Dia de los Muertos) is rooted in the Indigenous traditions of Mesoamerica. People create altars decorated with marigolds, photos and prized possessions of those lost. At North Lake we covered the prison’s entrance with banners and photos of those who had died and set up an altar. The ceremony included songs, messages from those who had been detained and deported from North Lake as well as from a statement from Mario David Coronado Juárez’s family. The names of those who died at the hands of ICE and its network were read out as participants called out presente after each name and shared a simple meal. A statement of intention opened the ceremony and a call to action ended it. Then we marched to the west side of the fence, where it was possible for those incarcerated to see and hear us. We chanted and sang until darkness fell. Althea Mukes from our chapter took extensive photos and video. Her impressive five-minute video was shown at Metro Detroit’s DSA meeting. For Metro Detroit DSA and our coalition partners, the action signifies a many-faceted campaign to force ICE out of Michigan. Given that North Lake is more than three hours from Detroit and in a rural area, we realize it may be difficult to return until next spring. We would like to project a larger action for next April. A speaker at the Dia de los Muertos event holding a sign with anti-ICE demands. In the meantime, we want to protest the county jails in our area that participate with ICE. We also encourage members to pledge a monthly contribution for those imprisoned at North Lake so they can obtain food and health products from the commissary. Members are also invited to writing letters (especially in Spanish!) to those we know are trapped at North Lake. Our solidarity is important as we build a campaign to abolish ICE! Please consider donating to the North Lake Comissary. Going to North Lake was originally published in The Detroit Socialist on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

articles.title: Sherrod Brown: Vote out Chuck Schumer!
articles.author: Columbus DSA
articles.content: A joint statement from the following Ohio DSA Chapters: Akron, Cleveland, Columbus, Dayton-Miami Valley, Mahoning Valley, Metro Cincinnati & Northern Kentucky, Wooster, Bowling Green O.C., Wheeling O.C. These Ohio Chapters of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) endorse the campaign led by the DSA National Electoral Commission (NEC) to Say No to Chuck Schumer as Senate Majority Leader . During his nearly three decades as a US Senator, Chuck Schumer has consistently advanced the interests of corporate power at home and imperialism abroad against the interests of working people. Under Obama, Schumer was among the few Democratic Senators to cross party lines and vote against the negotiated agreement between the United States and Iran. Serving during the Biden administration as Majority Leader, Schumer failed to codify Roe v. Wade into law, setting the stage for its overturning by the Supreme Court. Moreover, he failed to deliver meaningful legislation on important issues such as voting rights, worker rights, and climate change. Schumer participated in fearmongering against our immigrant neighbors and attempted to expand militant border security. Meanwhile, he has pledged that his top priority is to ensure the Democrats remain steadfast in their support of Israeli apartheid – despite the ongoing genocide in Gaza – and has received $1.7 million from pro-Israel groups since 1990, according to Open Secrets . As Minority Leader under the second Trump administration, Schumer has not used the congressional war powers to stop illegal wars abroad. Schumer has no intention of abolishing ICE – a moral imperative and the majority opinion of workers across the country. When Democrats used their leverage to force a historic government shutdown to preserve healthcare subsidies under the Affordable Care Act, Schumer capitulated – leading to dramatically increased costs for working people. The people have overwhelmingly demanded change while Chuck Schumer personifies complacency, cowardice, and corruption. If the Senate Democratic Caucus doesn’t take this opportunity to look toward new leadership and follow through on their promises to their constituents, then they would prove yet again that they do not represent the working class. We call on Sherrod Brown to vote against Chuck Schumer for Majority Leader because Workers Deserve More. Send a letter to Sherrod Brown telling him to “chuck Chuck” here .
